title: Module: Sidechain Compression - Explanation
content:
Understanding Sidechain Compression

In standard compression, the compressor monitors the volume of the audio track it is placed on. In Sidechain Compression, the compressor reacts to the volume of a different track (the key input).

Key Parameters

  • Threshold: The level the key input must reach to trigger gain reduction.
  • Ratio: How intensely the audio is reduced once triggered.
  • Attack: How quickly the compressor reacts to the key input.
  • Release: How quickly the audio returns to normal volume after the key input stops.

Edexcel Context (AO4)

Edexcel frequently tests sidechain gating and compression. In EDM, it is heavily used to 'duck' a bass or synth track whenever the kick drum hits, preventing low-frequency masking and creating a rhythmic 'pumping' effect.

title: Practical Task: Sidechain Compression
content:
Your DAW Mission

Download the provided stems below and complete the following task inside your DAW.

Task: Apply sidechain compression to the Synth Chords track, using the Kick Drum as the key input. The chords must duck rhythmically with the kick.

  • Step 1: Import the Kick and Synth Chords stems into your DAW.
  • Step 2: Place a compressor on the Synth Chords track.
  • Step 3: Route the Kick Drum track to the sidechain (key) input of the compressor.
  • Step 4: Adjust the threshold, ratio, and release time until you achieve a clear, rhythmic pumping effect without unnatural clicks.

Marking Criteria (Levels-Based)

  • Level 3 (3 marks): Synth chords duck cleanly exactly when the kick hits. Release time is musical and matches the tempo. No audio glitches.
  • Level 2 (2 marks): Rhythm is generally correct but the ducking is too extreme/too subtle, or release time is slightly too long.
  • Level 1 (1 mark): Sidechain is present but other bars are affected or incorrect rhythm.

Assets Required (Teacher Prep): kick_drum.wav, synth_chords.wav (120 BPM)

title: Knowledge Check: Sidechain Compression
description: A quick test to verify your Component 4 knowledge on dynamic processing before advancing.

questions.title: Q1: Release Time Analysis
questions.content: When configuring a sidechain compressor to create a 'pumping' effect on a synth bass, what is the most likely result of setting the release time too fast?

answers.text: The bass will sound distorted and produce unnatural clicking (artefacts).
The bass will remain permanently quiet and not return to its original volume.
The kick drum will become louder in the mix.
The compressor will stop reacting to the key input entirely.

questions.expert_explanation: AO4: If the release time is too fast, the compressor stops reducing gain before the low-frequency waveform of the bass has completed a cycle, causing waveform distortion and audible clicking.

questions.title: Q2: Signal Routing
questions.content: In a DAW, how is sidechain compression fundamentally different from standard compression?

answers.text: It uses an external audio signal to trigger the gain reduction on the target track.
It only compresses the high frequencies of a signal.
It requires a ratio of infinity:1 to function correctly.
It is applied directly to the master bus rather than individual tracks.

questions.expert_explanation: AO3: Sidechaining relies on routing a 'key input' (an external signal) into the detector circuit of the compressor, rather than having the compressor react to the track it is placed on.

questions.title: Q3: Purpose in Mixing
questions.content: Which of the following is a primary mixing reason to use sidechain compression between a kick drum and a bass guitar?

answers.text: To prevent low-frequency masking and ensure the kick transient cuts through.
To add harmonic saturation and warmth to the bass guitar.
To increase the overall dynamic range of the rhythm section.
To artificially lengthen the decay of the kick drum.

questions.expert_explanation: AO4: Because the kick and bass share the same low-frequency range, they often mask each other. Sidechaining ducks the bass for a fraction of a second when the kick hits, creating space for the kick's transient.
